safetyNote: Poisonous. Amanita proxima can cause delayed gastrointestinal illness followed by severe acute kidney injury. If ingestion is suspected, seek urgent poison-centre or emergency medical advice, even if symptoms have not started. Do not identify an edible amanita by volva colour alone.

sections.title: Identification
sections.text: A large, predominantly white to ivory amanita. The smooth cap may be faintly ochre at the centre. Crowded white gills are free from the stem. The white stem is often finely floccose, with a broad, persistent membranous ring. At its base is a conspicuous sac-like volva, typically ochre to rusty brown. Keep the entire stem base for examination.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: A Mediterranean species in woods and at woodland edges, associated especially with oaks and also reported with pines. It fruits mainly in autumn, often on calcareous ground.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Amanita ovoidea is another large pale amanita; its volva is generally whitish and its ring more fragile and creamy. These features can vary with age and weather, so colour alone cannot establish a safe identification. Other white Amanita species include dangerously poisonous taxa.

sections.title: Poisoning
sections.text: This species is associated with proxima syndrome: gastrointestinal symptoms may be followed by acute kidney injury. A 2024 clinical series of 13 attributed cases reported kidney replacement treatment in every patient. The DGfM lists it in the nephrotoxic Amanita group and notes that allenic norleucine has not yet been detected in this species; its exact toxic mechanism should not be treated as settled.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The white-background plate shows the whole fruit body with the ochre-russet volval sac intact, a longitudinal section, a cap seen from above, and the free white gills seen from below. These are illustrative views, not a substitute for expert identification.
